Mini-Lesson

Theme D: St Mark's Gospel: the life of Jesus (part 1)

7 missions. Guess, learn, then check. Your place is saved.

  1. Mission 1Why should a short book written 2,000 years ago still guide anyone's life today?
  2. Mission 2Why would someone Christians call sinless queue up to be baptised for forgiveness?
  3. Mission 3Why would fishermen drop their nets on the spot to follow a stranger?
  4. Mission 4If a storm stops or a crowd is fed, does it matter whether it really happened?
  5. Mission 5A frightened woman, a desperate father, a blind beggar: what did their faith have to do with healing?
  6. Mission 6Jesus healed people and taught about God. Why did powerful people want him dead?
  7. Mission 7Peter gets the answer right, then gets told off. What did he misunderstand?
Mission 1

Mission 1: Why should a short book written 2,000 years ago still guide anyone's life today?

Make a guess: Why should a short book written 2,000 years ago still guide anyone's life today?

Mission 1

What Mark is

  • "The beginning of the Good News of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." (Mark 1:1)
  • Gospel means "good news". Mark is not a modern biography: it proclaims who Jesus is.
  • Most scholars think Mark is the earliest of the four Gospels, written about 65–75 CE.
  • Matthew and Luke seem to use Mark as a main source (Markan priority).
  • Short and fast: Jesus acts "immediately"; the story drives towards the cross in Jerusalem.
Mission 1

Who wrote it, and for whom?

  • The Gospel does not name its author. Early tradition names John Mark, a companion of Peter and Paul (Acts 12:12; 1 Peter 5:13).
  • Papias (bishop of Hierapolis, c. 60–c. 130), quoted by Eusebius (Church History 3.39, c. 325): Mark was Peter's interpreter and wrote down accurately what he remembered, though not in order (paraphrase).
  • Audience: probably Gentile (non-Jewish) Christians. Mark explains Jewish customs (7:3–4) and translates Aramaic: "Talitha cumi!" … "Girl, I tell you, get up!" (Mark 5:41).
  • Setting: tradition says Rome, perhaps after Nero's persecution of Christians (64 CE).
  • Purpose: to show Jesus is the Christ and Son of God (1:1; 15:39), and to encourage followers facing suffering.
Quick check
?Which piece of evidence best supports the view that Mark wrote mainly for non-Jewish readers?
Mission 1

Three kinds of authority

  • Christians: Mark is part of scripture, inspired by God: "Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching" (2 Timothy 3:16).
  • Catholic teaching: scripture is read within Tradition, and the Church's teaching office (the Magisterium) interprets it (Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum, 1965, paraphrase).
  • Many evangelical Christians: scripture is the supreme authority; some hold it is without error in all it affirms (inerrancy).
  • Liberal Christians: an inspired but human witness; its truths are spiritual and moral more than scientific or historical.
  • Non-religious people (atheists, Humanists): a historical source and a work of ethics and literature, not the word of God.
Mission 1Diversity

One text, many readings

  • Varied interpretations of Mark's passages create diversity within Christianity:
  • The Last Supper (Mark 14:22–24): Catholics and Orthodox believe the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood; many Protestants see a memorial.
  • The rich man (Mark 10:17–27): monks, nuns and friars take vows of poverty; most Christians read it as a call to put God before wealth.
  • The ending of Mark: the oldest manuscripts end at 16:8; verses 9–20 were added later. Catholics and many others accept them as scripture; some Protestant scholars give them less weight.
  • Miracles: read as history, as history with meaning, or as symbolic stories (next screens).
Mission 1

Three lenses for any event in Mark

  • AQA asks why each event mattered for Jesus, for the people of his day, and for 21st-century people.
  • For Jesus: what it shows of his identity and mission (e.g. baptism: his calling).
  • For his day: what it meant to Jews under Roman rule, to the disciples, to the early Church (e.g. hope of a Messiah).
  • For today: how Christians worship, pray or act because of it (e.g. baptism services), and what non-religious people might take from it.
  • You will use these lenses in every Mark mission.
Mission 1

Teacher and miracle worker

  • Mark has fewer long sermons than Matthew or Luke, but many miracles: healings, exorcisms and nature miracles.
  • As teacher, Jesus speaks with his own authority, in parables and short sayings; people call him "Rabbi" and "Teacher".
  • As miracle worker, he shows power over illness, evil spirits, nature and death.
  • The two belong together: miracles show the authority behind the teaching, and show the Kingdom of God arriving (Mark 1:15).
  • Mark also shows Jesus refusing to give a "sign" to those who test him (8:11–12): miracles answer faith rather than prove it.
Mission 1Read the source

Authority

"They were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as having authority, and not as the scribes." (Mark 1:22)

"What is this? What can this new doctrine be? For with authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him!" (Mark 1:27)

Q1 How was Jesus' teaching different from the scribes'?

Show answer

He taught on his own authority, not by quoting earlier teachers.

Q2 How does verse 27 link the teacher and the miracle worker?

Show answer

The same authority shows in his words and in his power over evil spirits.

Mission 1Diversity

Did the miracles happen?

  • Literal: they happened as described; God can act in the world (most Catholic, Orthodox and evangelical Christians).
  • Historical core: Jesus did heal and amaze people, but the stories were shaped as they were retold.
  • Symbolic: the stories mainly teach truths (Jesus brings calm, feeds, frees). Rudolf Bultmann (1884–1976) urged reading the Gospels' message apart from their ancient world-view ("demythologising", 1941).
  • Non-religious: David Hume (1711–1776) argued that testimony to miracles is never strong enough to outweigh our experience of natural law (Enquiry, 1748). Many Humanists see the miracles as legend or misunderstood natural events.
  • Historical note: even Jesus' opponents in Mark do not deny his deeds; they claim his power comes from Beelzebul (3:22).
Quick check
?A Christian says: "Whether or not Jesus really walked on water, the story teaches me that he is with me in life's storms." Which view of the miracles does she hold?
Mission 1

Secular sources of authority

  • Secular sources of contemporary authority are not based on religion:
  • Science: evidence and testing; challenges miracle stories and some beliefs about the world.
  • Law and human rights: Parliament, courts, the Human Rights Act 1998.
  • Reason and conscience: each person thinking for themselves.
  • Majority opinion and media: what society accepts; influencers and news.
  • Christian responses: many see no conflict (science explains how, faith why); others say God's word must come first when they clash. Jesus' teaching (e.g. love your neighbour, Mark 12:31) is often supported by human rights law.
Mission 1

Can Mark speak to non-believers?

  • Britain's main religious tradition is Christian, but many people are atheists or Humanists.
  • Humanists may admire Jesus' example: care for outcasts (lepers, Levi), service (10:45), love your neighbour as yourself (12:31).
  • They accept it because it is reasonable and kind, not because of who Jesus is: ethical, not divine, authority.
  • Catholic response: the moral teaching cannot be separated from who Jesus is; Mark offers spiritual truth about God, sin and salvation, not just good advice.
  • So Mark can be "relevant" to non-believers, but its authority differs for them.
Mission 1Evaluate

"Mark's Gospel has no authority in 21st-century Britain."

  • Reasons for: science explains many events once seen as miracles; written decades after Jesus by someone who was not an eyewitness; law and human rights now guide public life; Britain is increasingly non-religious.
  • Reasons against: for millions of Christians it is inspired scripture, read in worship every Sunday; it may preserve Peter's memories (Papias); its teaching on love and service still shapes charities and law; even non-religious people respect its ethics.
  • Other view: authority comes in kinds: spiritual authority for believers, moral or literary for others.
  • Judge it by: Authority for whom? Is historical accuracy needed for spiritual truth? Can science and scripture answer different questions?
Mission check

?A modern charity's founding statement was written by its founder in 1985. A new manager argues the charity should now follow only government guidelines and opinion polls. Which pair of positions best mirrors the debate about Mark's authority?

Mark's authority depends on who is asking: inspired scripture for Christians, a source of history or ethics for others.

Mission 2

Mission 2: Why would someone Christians call sinless queue up to be baptised for forgiveness?

Make a guess: Why would someone Christians call sinless queue up to be baptised for forgiveness?

Mission 2

The messenger in the wilderness

  • Mark opens with prophecy: "Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you" (Mark 1:2, echoing Malachi 3:1) and "the voice of one crying in the wilderness" (Mark 1:3, echoing Isaiah 40:3).
  • John the Baptist is that messenger: he prepares people for someone greater.
  • He preached "the baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins" (Mark 1:4). Repentance means turning away from sin and back to God.
  • Crowds from Judea and Jerusalem came to the River Jordan, confessing their sins (1:5).
  • Clothing and food: camel's hair, a leather belt, locusts and wild honey (1:6). The belt recalls the prophet Elijah (2 Kings 1:8), whom Jews expected to return before God's day.
Mission 2Read the source

Someone mightier

"After me comes he who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and loosen. I baptised you in water, but he will baptise you in the Holy Spirit." (Mark 1:7–8)

  • Untying sandals was a slave's job: John says he is not fit even for that.

Q1 How does John compare himself with the one who is coming?

Show answer

He is lower than a slave to him.

Q2 What will the coming one do that John cannot?

Show answer

Baptise with the Holy Spirit, not only water.

Quick check
?Why do many Christians think Mark describes John's camel-hair clothing and leather belt?
Mission 2

The baptism of Jesus

  • Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptised by John in the Jordan (1:9).
  • Coming up from the water, "he saw the heavens parting and the Spirit descending on him like a dove." (Mark 1:10)
  • A voice: "You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." (Mark 1:11)
  • In Mark, Jesus himself sees and hears: it is addressed to him.
  • The words echo Psalm 2:7 (the king as God's son) and Isaiah 42:1 (God's chosen servant, on whom God puts his Spirit).
Mission 2

What the baptism shows

  • For Christians, the baptism shows:
  • Identity: Jesus is God's Son, approved by God.
  • Anointing: the Spirit comes on him; "Messiah" means "anointed one".
  • The start of the ministry: from here Jesus begins preaching (1:14–15).
  • The Trinity: Christians see Father (voice), Son (Jesus) and Holy Spirit (dove) together.
  • Solidarity: Christians believe Jesus was sinless, yet stood in line with sinners: he identifies with the people he came to save.
  • Example: he shows his followers the way of baptism.
Mission 2Diversity

The baptism for Christians today

  • Most churches baptise "in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit", using water.
  • Infant baptism (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Methodist): grace is God's gift before a person can choose; parents and godparents make promises.
  • Believer's baptism (Baptists, many Pentecostals and independent churches): only those old enough to repent and believe, often by full immersion, like Jesus in the Jordan.
  • Orthodox Christians celebrate the baptism at Theophany (6 January) with the blessing of waters.
  • Quakers and the Salvation Army do not baptise with water; they stress inner baptism by the Spirit (Mark 1:8).
Quick check
?In Mark's account of the baptism, which detail do Christians most often use to support belief in the Trinity?
Mission 2

The temptation

  • "Immediately the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness." (Mark 1:12)
  • Forty days, tempted by Satan, with the wild animals; angels served him (1:13).
  • Forty recalls Israel's forty years in the desert and the forty days of Moses (Exodus 34:28) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:8).
  • Mark gives no details and no result: Jesus' whole ministry becomes the battle with evil.
  • Significance: Jesus faces real temptation, so Christians believe he understands theirs: "one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15). Many Christians keep Lent, forty days of prayer and self-denial.
Mission 2Evaluate

"The baptism proves that Jesus is the Son of God."

  • Reasons for: a voice from heaven names him as Son; the Spirit descends; John, a prophet, says someone greater is coming; Christians across traditions read this as God's own testimony.
  • Reasons against (non-religious, e.g. atheist, Humanist): in Mark it is Jesus who sees the Spirit and the voice speaks to him, so it reads as a private experience that others cannot check; the account was written decades later by believers; a dove and a voice could be later symbolic language.
  • Christian responses: the story is a revelation to be received in faith, not a scientific proof; its meaning is confirmed by Jesus' whole life, death and resurrection; the centurion's words at the cross, "Truly this man was the Son of God!" (15:39), echo it.
  • Judge it by: What would count as "proof" of a religious claim? Is a private experience evidence for others? Does the story aim to prove or to proclaim?
Mission 2Worked answer

Belief, source, development

Question: Explain two ways the baptism of Jesus is significant for Christians today.

  • Way 1: it shows who Jesus is. Source: "You are my beloved Son" (Mark 1:11). Development: Christians worship Jesus as the Son of God, the second person of the Trinity.
  • Way 2: it is an example to follow. Development: Christians are baptised as Jesus was; Baptists do this by full immersion as believers, while Catholics baptise infants into God's family.
Mission check

?A new head teacher is introduced at assembly. The chair of governors says: "This is the person we have chosen, and we are delighted with her." From then on, she runs the school. Which part of Mark 1:1–13 does this most closely mirror, and why?

For Christians, the baptism marks Jesus out as God's beloved Son and launches his ministry; the temptation shows him facing evil before he begins.

Mission 3

Mission 3: Why would fishermen drop their nets on the spot to follow a stranger?

Make a guess: Why would fishermen drop their nets on the spot to follow a stranger?

Mission 3

"Immediately they left their nets"

  • By the Sea of Galilee Jesus sees Simon (Peter) and Andrew fishing.
  • "Come after me, and I will make you into fishers for men." (Mark 1:17)
  • "Immediately they left their nets, and followed him." (Mark 1:18)
  • James and John leave their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men (1:19–20).
  • Normally a student chose a rabbi. Here Jesus chooses them.
Mission 3

The call of Levi

  • Jesus sees Levi, a tax collector, at his booth: "Follow me." Levi gets up and follows (Mark 2:14).
  • Tax collectors worked for Rome or Herod Antipas, often overcharged, and were seen as traitors and unclean.
  • Jesus eats at Levi's house with "tax collectors and sinners". Scribes and Pharisees object.
  • "Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." (Mark 2:17)
  • Discipleship is open to outsiders: no one is too far gone to be called.
Quick check
?What did the Pharisees' objection at Levi's house show about religious attitudes in Jesus' day?
Mission 3

Rejected at Nazareth

  • Jesus teaches in his home town's synagogue. People are amazed, then offended.
  • "Isn't this the carpenter, the son of Mary…?" (Mark 6:3): they think they know him too well.
  • "A prophet is not without honour, except in his own country, and amongst his own relatives, and in his own house." (Mark 6:4)
  • "He could do no mighty work there", except heal a few sick people (6:5).
  • He "marvelled because of their unbelief" (6:6): in Mark, miracles are often linked to faith.
Quick check
?Why, according to Mark 6:1–6, could Jesus do few mighty works in Nazareth?
Mission 3Read the source

Sent out two by two

"He called to himself the twelve, and began to send them out two by two; and he gave them authority over the unclean spirits. He commanded them that they should take nothing for their journey, except a staff only: no bread, no wallet, no money in their purse." (Mark 6:7–8)

  • They may wear sandals but not two tunics; they stay in one house; where rejected, they "shake off the dust" from their feet (6:9–11).
  • They preach repentance, cast out demons and anoint the sick with oil (6:12–13).

Q1 What are the Twelve allowed to take?

Show answer

A staff and sandals, and one tunic.

Q2 What three things do they do?

Show answer

Preach repentance, cast out demons, heal the sick.

Mission 3

What the mission shows

  • Shared authority: Jesus' power to teach and heal is passed to his followers.
  • Dependence: taking nothing means trusting God and the hospitality of others.
  • Urgency: travel light, move on; there is no time to waste.
  • Two by two: support and a reliable witness (two witnesses in Jewish law, Deuteronomy 19:15).
  • Preach and serve: words (repentance) and actions (healing) go together.
  • Rejection is expected: shaking off dust is a sign, not revenge: the message was offered.
Quick check
?A student says, "Jesus told the Twelve to take nothing because he wanted them to suffer." Which response best fits Mark 6:7–13?
Mission 3Diversity

Following the call today

  • Catholic: every baptised person is a "missionary disciple" (Pope Francis, Evangelii Gaudium, 2013, paraphrase); some answer a call to priesthood or religious life.
  • Religious orders take the mission of the Twelve literally: Franciscans and others vow poverty and depend on others.
  • Many Protestants stress that every Christian is called where they are (the "priesthood of all believers"): at work, at school, at home.
  • Evangelical and Pentecostal Christians stress telling others about Jesus; Pentecostals also pray for healing.
  • Humanists admire commitment and service but question leaving family and work for a belief they see as unproven.
Mission 3Worked answer

Belief, source, development

Question: Explain two lessons about discipleship from the call of the first disciples. Refer to St Mark's Gospel in your answer.

  • Lesson 1: discipleship means an immediate, total response. Source: "Immediately they left their nets, and followed him" (Mark 1:18). Development: Christians today put Jesus before work and comfort, e.g. giving time to serve others.
  • Lesson 2: disciples are sent to bring others to God. Source: "I will make you into fishers for men" (1:17). Development: so Christians share their faith by word and example.
  • 5-mark tip: two lessons, each developed, plus a reference to Mark.
Mission check

?A charity sends volunteers into a new town in pairs, with no money, to stay with local families and offer free help. Which instruction from the mission of the Twelve does the "no money" rule mirror most closely?

The call is personal and immediate; the mission is shared, dependent on God, and open to rejection.

Mission 4

Mission 4: If a storm stops or a crowd is fed, does it matter whether it really happened?

Make a guess: If a storm stops or a crowd is fed, does it matter whether it really happened?

Mission 4

What is a nature miracle?

  • A miracle in the Gospels is an act of power. Mark calls them "mighty works" and presents them as showing God at work.
  • Nature miracles: Jesus shows power over the natural world (wind, sea, food), not only over illness or evil spirits.
  • In the Jewish scriptures, only God rules the sea and feeds his people in the wilderness.
  • So the question each story raises is: who is this?
  • Many Christians see Jesus' miracles as signs that God's Kingdom has come near (1:15); in Mark they call for faith.
Mission 4

Feeding the five thousand

  • The Twelve return from their mission; Jesus takes them to a quiet place to rest (6:30–31).
  • A crowd follows. Jesus "had compassion on them because they were like sheep without a shepherd" (Mark 6:34) and teaches them.
  • Disciples: send them away to buy food. Jesus: "You give them something to eat." (Mark 6:37)
  • Five loaves and two fish. "He took the five loaves and the two fish; and looking up to heaven, he blessed and broke the loaves, and he gave to his disciples to set before them" (Mark 6:41).
  • "They all ate and were filled." Twelve baskets left over; five thousand men ate (6:42–44).
  • Took, blessed, broke, gave: Mark uses the same four actions with bread at the Last Supper (14:22).
  • Echoes: God feeding Israel with manna (Exodus 16); the prophet Elisha feeding a hundred, with some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44); the shepherd of Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34.
Quick check
?In the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus took the loaves, "blessed and broke" them and gave them. Why do many Christians link this with the Last Supper?
Mission 4Diversity

What do the nature miracles show?

  • Identity: for Christians, Jesus has God's power over nature, so they see him as the Son of God.
  • Compassion: he feeds the hungry and cares for the frightened.
  • The Messiah's banquet: Jews hoped for a great feast in God's Kingdom; the feeding is a foretaste.
  • Interpretations among Christians:
  • Literal: real events; God, who made nature, can act in it (Catholic, Orthodox and many evangelical Christians).
  • Sharing: some liberal Christians suggest the crowd shared food they had hidden; the "miracle" was generosity.
  • Symbolic: stories that teach trust in Christ in hard times, and point to the Eucharist.
  • Significance today: trust in God in crisis; the Eucharist; Christian charities such as CAFOD, Christian Aid and Tearfund "give them something to eat".
Mission 4

Non-religious arguments

  • Natural explanations: the crowd may simply have shared food they had brought.
  • David Hume (1711–1776): testimony to miracles is never strong enough to outweigh the uniform experience of nature; and miracle stories "are observed chiefly to abound among ignorant and barbarous nations" (An Enquiry concerning Human Understanding, 1748, Section X).
  • Late and biased witnesses: the stories were written decades later by believers.
  • No proof of divinity: in the Bible, prophets such as Elisha also work wonders; Mark warns that false messiahs will show "signs and wonders" (13:22).
  • Humanists usually see the miracles as legend or symbolic stories.
Quick check
?Which statement is a non-religious argument against the nature miracles, rather than a Christian interpretation of them?
Mission 4Evaluate

"The nature miracles must have really happened for them to matter to Christians."

  • Reasons for: Christians claim Jesus is divine; if he did not have God's power, the stories mislead. Mark presents them as events, with places and numbers. Paul says faith is empty if Christ is not raised (1 Corinthians 15:14, paraphrase); many apply the same logic to miracles.
  • Reasons against: Jesus refuses to give a "sign" to prove himself (8:11–12); the stories' message (trust, compassion, the Eucharist) holds even if read symbolically; many Christians' faith rests on the resurrection and on experience of God, not on these stories.
  • Christian responses to science: a natural cause and God's action are not rivals (God can act through nature and its timing); laws describe what usually happens, not what God must do.
  • Judge it by: Can a story be true in meaning without being literal? What does "proof" mean in religion? Is Hume's standard of evidence fair to unique events?
Mission 4Worked answer

Two contrasting beliefs

Question: Explain two contrasting beliefs about the feeding of the five thousand.

  • Belief 1: It really happened as Mark says. Development: God's Son has power over creation, so Jesus multiplied the bread (Mark 6:41–44); Catholic and many evangelical Christians hold this.
  • Belief 2: It is a story of sharing, or a symbol. Development: the crowd shared their food, or the story points to the Eucharist; some liberal Christians and many non-religious people take this view.
  • 4-mark tip: two contrasting beliefs, each developed; a source is not required here (the 5-mark question asks for one).
Mission check

?A firefighter rescues a child moments before a bridge collapses. The child's mother says, "That was God." A scientist says, "That was training and luck." Which response is most like the view of many Christians about Mark's nature miracles?

Christians differ on how literally to read the nature miracles, but agree that they point to who Jesus is.

Mission 5

Mission 5: A frightened woman, a desperate father, a blind beggar: what did their faith have to do with healing?

Make a guess: A frightened woman, a desperate father, a blind beggar: what did their faith have to do with healing?

Mission 5

Healing as a sign

  • Mark calls them mighty works (6:5). Many Christians see them as signs that God's Kingdom has come near (1:15).
  • The prophets pictured that time: "Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped." (Isaiah 35:5)
  • Mark's healings show Jesus' compassion and his authority: he acts by his own word and touch.
  • They often call for faith: trust in Jesus and in God's power.
  • They often break a barrier: sickness, uncleanness, death, being pushed aside.
Mission 5

The paralysed man

  • Capernaum: the house is packed. Four friends dig through the roof and lower their friend on his mat (2:1–4).
  • "Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, 'Son, your sins are forgiven you.'" (Mark 2:5)
  • Some scribes think: only God can forgive sins; this is blasphemy (2:6–7).
  • Jesus heals the man so "that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" (2:10).
  • The man walks out carrying his mat; everyone glorifies God (2:12).
  • Faith here is the friends' faith, shown in action.
Mission 5

Jairus' daughter

  • Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, falls at Jesus' feet: his little daughter is dying (5:22–23).
  • On the way, a delay (the woman, next screen). Then news: "Your daughter is dead." (5:35)
  • Jesus: "Don't be afraid, only believe." (Mark 5:36)
  • He takes only Peter, James and John and the parents. Mourners laugh at "not dead, but … asleep" (5:39–40).
  • "Talitha cumi!" (Aramaic: "Girl, I tell you, get up!"). She gets up and walks; she is twelve (5:41–42).
  • He orders silence and tells them to give her something to eat (5:43).
Mission 5

The woman with a haemorrhage

  • Bleeding for twelve years; she has spent everything on doctors and grown worse (5:25–26).
  • Under the Law, her bleeding made her ritually unclean (Leviticus 15:25), cut off from worship and touch.
  • She thinks: "If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well." (Mark 5:28) She is healed at once.
  • Jesus stops: "Who touched my clothes?" She comes forward, "fearing and trembling", and tells the whole truth (5:30–33).
  • He calls her "Daughter": healed in body, and welcomed back in public.
  • Mark sandwiches her story inside Jairus' story: a leader and an outcast, both twelve years, both "daughters".
Mission 5Read the source

"Your faith has made you well"

"He said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be cured of your disease.'" (Mark 5:34)

"But Jesus, when he heard the message spoken, immediately said to the ruler of the synagogue, 'Don't be afraid, only believe.'" (Mark 5:36)

Q1 Whose faith does Jesus praise in 5:34?

Show answer

The woman's: her trust that led her to reach out.

Q2 When is Jairus asked to believe?

Show answer

After hearing his daughter is dead: faith when all seems lost.

Quick check
?Why do many Christians think Mark places the woman's healing in the middle of the story of Jairus' daughter?
Mission 5

Bartimaeus

  • Leaving Jericho, on the way to Jerusalem. A blind beggar sits by the road (10:46).
  • He shouts: "Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!" (Mark 10:47) Son of David: a title for the Messiah.
  • The crowd tells him to be quiet; he shouts louder (10:48). Persistent faith.
  • He throws off his cloak (perhaps all he owns) and comes (10:50).
  • "Rabboni, that I may see again." Jesus: "Go your way. Your faith has made you well." (10:51–52)
  • He "followed Jesus on the way" (10:52): he becomes a disciple, on the road to the cross.
  • He sees clearly, while the disciples, just before, have misunderstood (10:35–45).
Quick check
?Bartimaeus calls Jesus "son of David" and then "followed Jesus on the way". What do many Christians see in this?
Mission 5Diversity

What is faith in Mark?

  • Trust in Jesus' power: the woman and Jairus believe he can heal (5:28, 5:36).
  • Faith that acts: the friends break a roof (2:4); Bartimaeus will not be silenced (10:48).
  • Faith of others: the man is healed through his friends' faith (2:5), the girl through her father's.
  • Faith that struggles: "I believe. Help my unbelief!" (9:24, a later mission).
  • Unbelief limits: at Nazareth "he could do no mighty work there", and "marvelled because of their unbelief" (6:5–6).
  • Different views: some Christians stress faith as trust in Jesus; others as commitment, following him (Bartimaeus); some stress that God's grace comes first, and faith is a response.
  • Many Christians reject the claim that people who are not healed simply "lacked faith": Jesus also heals where faith is not mentioned (1:34).
Mission 5Diversity

Healing miracles today

  • Literal: real events; Jesus has God's power over sickness and death (Catholic, Orthodox, many Protestants).
  • Catholic practice: the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick (James 5:14–15); pilgrimage to Lourdes, where the Church recognises a small number of healings as miracles after medical review.
  • Pentecostal and charismatic churches hold healing services and pray for healing with laying on of hands.
  • Liberal readings: healing of mind and body together; the stories mainly teach inclusion and wholeness.
  • Christian witness: hospitals, hospices and medical missions continue Jesus' care.
  • Non-religious views: stories grew in retelling; some illnesses may improve through belief (the placebo effect); Humanists value the compassion but not the miraculous claim.
Mission 5Evaluate

"In Mark's healing miracles, faith matters more than the miracle itself."

  • Reasons for: Jesus says "your faith has made you well" (5:34; 10:52). Bartimaeus' healing ends in following. Unbelief at Nazareth limits him (6:5–6). The woman gains more than health: a name, "Daughter".
  • Reasons against: the miracles show who Jesus is: only God forgives sins (2:7–10). Jesus heals where no faith is mentioned (1:34). The girl is dead: she can have no faith. The healings are signs of the Kingdom (Isaiah 35:5–6).
  • Non-religious view: if the miracles did not happen, the stories still show compassion and courage, but no special power.
  • Judge it by: Does faith cause the healing or receive it? Is Mark's main point who Jesus is, or how to respond to him? Does it matter whether the events are historical?
Mission check

?A charity offers free eye operations in a remote village. One woman walks two days to reach the clinic, ignoring neighbours who tell her it is a waste of time. How is she most like a person in Mark's healing stories?

In Mark, faith is trust that reaches out, keeps going and then follows; the healings show who Jesus is and invite that response.

Mission 6

Mission 6: Jesus healed people and taught about God. Why did powerful people want him dead?

Make a guess: Jesus healed people and taught about God. Why did powerful people want him dead?

Mission 6

Who were the authorities?

  • Scribes: experts who copied, taught and interpreted the Law of Moses.
  • Pharisees: a respected movement of devout Jews who applied the Law carefully to daily life, especially purity and the Sabbath.
  • Herodians: supporters of Herod's family, who ruled under Rome.
  • Chief priests: ran the Temple in Jerusalem; with elders and scribes they formed the Sanhedrin (council).
  • Romans: the occupying power; the Gospels present only the governor as able to order an execution (John 18:31).
  • In Mark, these groups clash with Jesus over authority: who speaks for God?
Mission 6

The first conflict: forgiving sins

  • A paralysed man is lowered through a roof. Jesus says: "Son, your sins are forgiven you." (Mark 2:5)
  • Scribes think: "Why does this man speak blasphemies like that? Who can forgive sins but God alone?" (Mark 2:7)
  • Blasphemy: insulting God, or claiming what belongs only to God.
  • Jesus heals the man "that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" (2:10).
  • For Christians this shows Jesus' divine authority. For the scribes, it was a serious offence.
  • It opens a chain of five disputes (2:1–3:6) that ends in a plot to kill him (3:6).
Quick check
?Why did some scribes accuse Jesus of blasphemy when he healed the paralysed man?
Mission 6

Why conflict drives Mark's story

  • Conflict grows: questions (2:7) → watching to accuse (3:2) → a plot (3:6) → the leaders seek to destroy him (11:18) → arrest and trial (14).
  • The later clashes in brief: on the Sabbath his disciples pick grain and he heals a man in the synagogue, while opponents watch to accuse him and then plot (3:2, 3:6); in Jerusalem he drives traders from the Temple, and the chief priests seek to destroy him (11:18).
  • Each clash is about authority: to forgive, over the Sabbath, over the Temple.
  • The conflicts show who Jesus is (Son of Man, with God's authority) and why he died.
  • They prepare readers for the cross, which Jesus foretells three times (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34).
  • Fairness: these were debates among Jews; Jesus and his disciples were Jews; crowds of Jews followed him.
  • Christian churches today reject blaming the Jewish people for Jesus' death (Catholic Church, Nostra Aetate, 1965).
Mission check

?A film-maker adapting Mark's Gospel wants to cut the arguments with the authorities and keep only the miracles. Which reason would a Christian scholar most likely give for keeping them?

In Mark, every conflict is about authority, and each one brings Jesus closer to the cross.

Mission 7

Mission 7: Peter gets the answer right, then gets told off. What did he misunderstand?

Make a guess: Peter gets the answer right, then gets told off. What did he misunderstand?

Mission 7

A turning point at Caesarea Philippi

  • Caesarea Philippi: a city in the far north, near the source of the Jordan, with a shrine to the Greek god Pan and a temple honouring the Roman emperor.
  • A place of other gods and Roman power: a striking setting to ask who Jesus really is.
  • It falls near the middle of Mark. Before it, Jesus' power is shown; after it, the road leads to the cross in Jerusalem.
Mission 7Read the source

"Who do you say that I am?"

On the way, Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is. They answer: John the Baptiser, Elijah, or one of the prophets (Mark 8:27–28, paraphrase).

"But who do you say that I am?" Peter answered, "You are the Christ." (Mark 8:29)

Q1 What did other people think about Jesus?

Show answer

That he was John the Baptist, Elijah, or another prophet.

Q2 What did Peter see that the crowds did not?

Show answer

That Jesus is the Christ, the Messiah, not just a prophet.

Mission 7

The rebuke

  • Jesus "commanded them that they should tell no one about him." (Mark 8:30)
  • Then the first passion prediction: "the Son of Man must suffer many things… and be killed, and after three days rise again." (Mark 8:31)
  • Peter takes him aside and rebukes him (8:32).
  • Jesus: "Get behind me, Satan! For you have in mind not the things of God, but the things of men." (Mark 8:33)
  • Peter's title was right; his idea of the Messiah was wrong. He expected victory; Jesus teaches suffering, death and resurrection.
  • "Satan" here: Peter is tempting Jesus away from his path, as Satan did in the wilderness.
Quick check
?Why does Jesus call Peter "Satan" at Caesarea Philippi?
Mission 7

The transfiguration

  • After six days Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain.
  • He is "changed into another form"; his clothes become dazzling white (9:2–3).
  • Elijah and Moses appear, talking with him (9:4).
  • Peter, afraid, offers to build three tents (9:5–6).
  • A cloud overshadows them; a voice: "This is my beloved Son. Listen to him." (Mark 9:7)
  • Suddenly they see only Jesus (9:8).
Mission 7

Why Moses and Elijah?

  • Moses = the Law: the lawgiver who received the Torah on Mount Sinai, where the cloud of God's glory covered the mountain (Exodus 24:16).
  • Elijah = the Prophets: the great prophet, who met God on Mount Horeb; expected to return: "I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes." (Malachi 4:5)
  • Together they stand for the whole Jewish scriptures. Christians believe Jesus fulfils both.
  • "Listen to him" recalls Moses' promise of a prophet like himself: "You shall listen to him." (Deuteronomy 18:15)
  • Coming down (9:9): tell no one until the Son of Man has risen.
Quick check
?Why do Christians think Moses and Elijah appear at the transfiguration?
Mission 7

What the transfiguration shows

  • For Christians, the transfiguration shows:
  • Identity: God's own voice calls Jesus "my beloved Son", as at the baptism.
  • Glory: the three disciples glimpse his divine glory before the suffering ahead.
  • Authority: "Listen to him": his teaching, including about suffering, carries God's authority.
  • Link with Caesarea Philippi: Peter has just heard that the Messiah must suffer; now he sees that suffering is not the end.
  • Resurrection: the glory points ahead to Easter.
Mission 7Diversity

The transfiguration today

  • Orthodox Christians celebrate it as a major feast (6 August); they see in the light on the mountain God's own uncreated glory, which believers can share (theosis: becoming like God by grace).
  • Catholics also keep 6 August, and pray it as one of the Luminous Mysteries of the Rosary (added 2002).
  • Many Protestants stress "Listen to him": the authority of Jesus' words, and encouragement in hard times.
  • Christians across traditions see it as a "mountain-top" experience that prepares for the "valley" of service.
Mission 7Evaluate

"The transfiguration proves that Jesus is the Messiah."

  • Reasons for: God's voice declares him Son; Moses and Elijah, the Law and Prophets, confirm him; three witnesses were present; it fits Jesus' resurrection.
  • Reasons against (non-religious, e.g. atheist, Humanist): a vision is a private experience; it may have been a dream, a mistake in a frightened state, or a story written later to express faith; three close followers are not neutral witnesses; visions occur in many religions with conflicting messages.
  • Christian responses: the transfiguration is not offered as proof but as revelation, received by faith; it is consistent with the whole story of Jesus, especially the resurrection; two of the three witnesses, James (Acts 12:2) and, by tradition, Peter, were later killed for their faith.
  • Judge it by: What counts as evidence for a religious claim? Can an experience be real but not provable? Did Mark intend it as proof or as proclamation?
Quick check
?At Caesarea Philippi Jesus predicts his suffering; at the transfiguration the disciples see his glory. How do many Christians link the two events?
Mission check

?A football coach tells a new player: "You've got the talent everyone talks about. But winning here means early mornings, injuries and sacrifice first." The player says: "No, that won't happen to us!" Which moment in Mark does this most closely mirror?

In Mark, Peter knows Jesus' title but not the path: the Messiah's glory comes through suffering.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Mark is probably the earliest Gospel (c. 65–75 CE), traditionally by John Mark from Peter's preaching, for Gentile Christians.
  • Christians give it authority as inspired scripture, interpreted in different ways; non-religious people may value its ethics but not its claims about God.
  • Views on the miracles range from literal to symbolic; secular sources (science, law, reason) challenge or support its authority.

Mission 2

  • John the Baptist is the messenger foretold by Malachi and Isaiah: he preaches repentance and points to one mightier than himself.
  • At the baptism the Spirit descends and the voice calls Jesus "my beloved Son": for Christians this reveals who he is, and his ministry begins.

Mission 3

  • Fishermen (Mark 1:16–20) and a tax collector (2:13–17) respond at once: Jesus calls ordinary people and outsiders.
  • The Twelve are sent two by two with nothing, to preach repentance and heal (6:7–13).
  • At Nazareth, familiarity and unbelief block Jesus' work (6:1–6).

Mission 4

  • In Mark, nature miracles show Jesus doing what, in the Jewish scriptures, only God does: stilling the sea, feeding his people in the wilderness.
  • Christians read them literally, as acts of sharing, or symbolically; non-religious people (Hume, Humanists) doubt the evidence and say they prove nothing about divinity.

Mission 5

  • Mark's healings are signs of God's Kingdom and show Jesus' compassion and authority, even over sin and death.
  • Faith in Mark is trust that acts (the friends, the woman, Jairus, Bartimaeus) and becomes following.
  • Christians read the healings literally, as wholeness and inclusion, or as continuing in prayer, sacraments and medicine; non-religious people doubt the miraculous.

Mission 6

  • Scribes, Pharisees, Herodians and chief priests clashed with Jesus over his authority: to forgive sins, over the Sabbath, over the Temple.
  • The conflicts explain why Jesus died; Christians read them as debates among Jews, not as blame on the Jewish people.

Mission 7

  • At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses "You are the Christ", but rebukes Jesus' prediction of suffering and is called "Satan".
  • At the transfiguration Jesus is changed in glory; Moses (the Law) and Elijah (the Prophets) appear; God says "This is my beloved Son. Listen to him."
